name: Trader test battery
models: Reported, as of Nov 2026: the Optiver, IMC and Citadel Securities test batteries. Number sequences, probability at speed, and likelihood ranking with intervals.
description: These are reported formats from the Optiver, IMC and Citadel Securities test batteries, as described by Nov 2026. There are three papers, each on its own clock. Sequences is 15 questions in 25 minutes, one at a time, with no skipping. Probability at speed is 15 questions in 30 minutes; you may move between them. Likelihood ranking and intervals is 10 questions in 10 minutes. Wrong answers score 0, and no calculator is allowed. Firms mix and rename these papers, so expect a different order on the day. This is version 1 of 3.

items.title: Equal gaps
items.question: What comes next? 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, ?

options.why: You doubled the last term. The gaps are equal, not the ratios.
You were one out. Check the last step again.
You added the gap of 4 twice.

feedback.correct: The gap is +4 each time.
feedback.generic: Find the gap between neighbours, with its sign.

explain.text: Each term is 4 more than the one before. So the next is $23 + 4 = 27$.

items.title: A constant ratio
items.question: What comes next? 2, 6, 18, 54, 162, ?

options.why: You added the last gap of 108 again. The gaps grow too.
You were one out. Multiply the last term again.
You multiplied by 2. Each term is 3 times the one before.

feedback.correct: Each term is 3 times the one before.
feedback.generic: Divide each term by the one before it.

explain.text: The ratio is 3 throughout. So the next is $3 \times 162 = 486$.

items.title: Squares shifted
items.question: What comes next? 5, 10, 17, 26, 37, ?

options.why: You added the last gap of 11 again. The gaps grow by 2.
You gave $7^2$ and dropped the +1.
You doubled the last term. The gaps grow by 2, so look for squares.

feedback.correct: Each term is a square plus 1: $7^2 + 1 = 50$.
feedback.generic: Compare each term with the nearest square.

explain.text: The terms are $n^2 + 1$ for $n = 2$ to $6$. The next is $7^2 + 1 = 50$. Check: the gaps rise by 2, so the next gap is 13.

items.title: Double and adjust
items.question: What comes next? 3, 5, 9, 17, 33, ?

options.why: You doubled and then added 1: the sign is wrong.
You doubled 33 and left out the −1.
You repeated the last gap of 16. The gaps double.

feedback.correct: Double, then take away 1.
feedback.generic: Try doubling each term and see what is left over.

explain.text: Each term is double the one before, minus 1. So the next is $2 \times 33 - 1 = 65$. Check: the gaps double, so the next gap is 32.

items.title: Growing gaps
items.question: What comes next? 2, 5, 11, 20, 32, ?

options.why: You repeated the last gap of 12. The gaps grow by 3.
You doubled the last term. Look at the gaps instead.
You were one out. Each gap is 3 more than the last.

feedback.correct: The gaps grow by 3: the next gap is 15.
feedback.generic: Write down the gaps, then the gaps between the gaps.

explain.text: The gaps are 3, 6, 9, 12, rising by 3 each time. So the next gap is 15 and the next term is $32 + 15 = 47$.

items.title: Two steps in turn
items.question: What comes next? 4, 8, 5, 10, 7, 14, ?

options.why: You repeated the last gap of 7.
You multiplied by 2 again. The steps take turns: $\times 2$, then $-3$.
You took away 2, not 3.

feedback.correct: The steps take turns, $\times 2$ then $-3$. Next is $- 3$.
feedback.generic: Look at the steps one at a time: they are not all the same kind.

explain.text: The steps go $\times 2$, $-3$, $\times 2$, $-3$ in turn. The next step is $- 3$, so $14 - 3 = 11$.

items.title: Sum of the two before
items.question: What comes next? 3, 4, 7, 11, 18, 29, ?

options.why: You doubled the last term. Add the two before instead.
You were one out. Add the last two terms again.
You repeated the last gap of 11.

feedback.correct: Each term is the sum of the two before: $18 + 29 = 47$.
feedback.generic: Add two neighbours and compare with the term after them.

explain.text: Each term is the sum of the two before it. So the next is $18 + 29 = 47$. Check: the gaps are the earlier terms, so the next gap is 18.

options.why: You carried on the last step, −6. The two lists take turns.
You applied the odd-place rule, +3. The eighth term is an even place.
You doubled the last term. The two lists take turns.

feedback.correct: Two lists take turns. The even places go −2, so $16 - 2 = 14$.
feedback.generic: Read every other term on its own.

explain.text: The odd places go 1, 4, 7, 10, and the even places go 20, 18, 16. The eighth term is an even place, so it is $16 - 2 = 14$.

options.why: You doubled the last term.
You were one out. Add the digits of the last term again.
You repeated the last gap of 7.

feedback.correct: Add the digit sum: $59 + 14 = 73$.
feedback.generic: Compare each gap with the digits of the term before it.

explain.text: Each gap is the digit sum of the term before: $19 + 10 = 29$, and so on. The last term 59 has digit sum 14, so the next is 73.

items.title: Primes
items.question: What comes next? 3, 5, 8, 11, 16, 19, ?

options.why: You took the next prime after 19. The terms are primes plus their place.
You doubled the last term.
You repeated the last gap of 3.

feedback.correct: The $n$th prime plus $n$: $17 + 7 = 24$.
feedback.generic: Subtract 1, 2, 3, ... from the terms and look again.

explain.text: The terms are $2 + 1$, $3 + 2$, $5 + 3$, and so on: the $n$th prime plus $n$. The 7th prime is 17, so the next is $17 + 7 = 24$.

items.title: Cubes shifted
items.question: What comes next? 6, 25, 62, 123, 214, ?

options.why: You doubled the last term. Compare the terms with the cubes.
You gave $7^3$ and dropped the −2.
You repeated the last gap of 91. The gaps grow faster each time.

feedback.correct: Each term is a cube minus 2: $7^3 - 2 = 341$.
feedback.generic: Compare each term with 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, ...

explain.text: The terms are $n^3 - 2$ for $n = 2$ to $6$. So the next is $7^3 - 2 = 343 - 2 = 341$.

options.why: You doubled 27, the odd-place term.
You applied the odd-place rule, $\times 3$. The eighth term is an even place.
You added the last two terms.

feedback.correct: The even places go $\times 2$, so $40 \times 2 = 80$.
feedback.generic: Read the odd places and the even places as two lists.

explain.text: The odd places go 1, 3, 9, 27 ($\times 3$). The even places go 10, 20, 40 ($\times 2$). The eighth term is an even place: $40 \times 2 = 80$.

items.title: Neighbours multiplied
items.question: What comes next? 6, 12, 20, 30, 42, ?

options.why: You squared 8. Each term is two neighbours multiplied.
You repeated the last gap of 12. The gaps grow by 2.
You doubled the last term.

feedback.correct: Each term is $n(n + 1)$: $7 \times 8 = 56$.
feedback.generic: Write each term as a product of two whole numbers close together.

explain.text: The terms are $2 \times 3$, $3 \times 4$, and so on. So the next is $7 \times 8 = 56$. Check: the gaps rise by 2, so the next gap is 14.

items.title: A rising multiplier
items.question: What comes next? 1, 2, 5, 16, 65, ?

options.why: You multiplied by 5 and left out the + 1.
You kept the multiplier at 4. It rises by 1 each step.
You repeated the last gap of 49.

feedback.correct: Multiply by a number that rises by 1 each step, then add 1: $5 \times 65 + 1 = 326$.
feedback.generic: Divide each term by the one before. What do the ratios do?

explain.text: The chain is $1 \times 1 + 1 = 2$, $2 \times 2 + 1 = 5$, $3 \times 5 + 1 = 16$, $4 \times 16 + 1 = 65$. The multiplier rises by 1 each step, so the next is $5 \times 65 + 1 = 326$.

items.title: Sum of the three before
items.question: What comes next? 1, 2, 3, 6, 11, 20, 37, ?

options.why: You added only the last two terms. Each term is the sum of three.
You doubled the last term.
You repeated the last gap of 17.

feedback.correct: Each term is the sum of the three before: $11 + 20 + 37 = 68$.
feedback.generic: Try adding two terms, then three, and compare with the next.

explain.text: From the fourth term on, each is the sum of the three before it. So the next is $11 + 20 + 37 = 68$. Check: $37 \times 2 - 6 = 68$ gives the same.

items.title: A total of 9
items.question: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the chance that the total is 9?

options.why: You treated the 11 totals as equally likely. A middle total has more ways.
You found the chance that the total is not 9.
You counted each pair twice. There are 4 ordered pairs, not 8.

feedback.correct: 4 of the 36 ordered pairs make 9.
feedback.generic: List the ordered pairs that make the total, out of 36.

explain.text: The pairs (3, 6), (4, 5), (5, 4), (6, 3) make 9. That is 4 of 36, so $\tfrac{1}{9}$.

items.title: Exactly 2 heads in 5
items.question: A fair coin is tossed 5 times. What is the chance of exactly 2 heads?

options.why: You counted ordered pairs of tosses, $5 \times 4 = 20$. There are $\binom{5}{2} = 10$ orders.
You took 2 heads out of 5 tosses as the chance.
You found the chance of anything but exactly 2 heads.

feedback.correct: $\binom{5}{2} = 10$ orders, each $\tfrac{1}{32}$.
feedback.generic: Count the orders, then multiply by the chance of one order.

explain.text: There are $\binom{5}{2} = 10$ orders, each with chance $\tfrac{1}{32}$. So the chance is $\tfrac{10}{32} = \tfrac{5}{16}$. Listing all 32 sequences finds the same 10.

items.title: At least one six in three
items.question: A fair die is rolled three times. What is the chance of at least one six?

options.why: You found the chance of no six at all.
You found the chance that every roll is a six.
You added $\tfrac16$ three times. That counts two sixes twice.

feedback.correct: One minus the chance of no six: $1 - \tfrac{125}{216}$.
feedback.generic: Find the chance of no six first.

explain.text: No six has chance $(\tfrac56)^3 = \tfrac{125}{216}$. So at least one six is $\tfrac{91}{216}$. Listing the 216 outcomes gives 91 with a six.

items.title: Red after red
items.question: Two cards are dealt from a full deck. The first is red. What is the chance that the second is red?

options.why: You found the chance that both are red, not the second given the first.
You took the card away but still counted 26 reds.
You put the first card back. With it gone, 25 of the 51 left are red.

feedback.correct: 25 reds are left among 51 cards.
feedback.generic: Take the first card out, then count what is left.

explain.text: After a red card, 25 of the 51 cards left are red, so $\tfrac{25}{51}$. Check: both red is $\tfrac{26}{52} \cdot \tfrac{25}{51}$, and dividing by $\tfrac12$ gives $\tfrac{25}{51}$.

items.title: Three of one suit
items.question: Three cards are dealt from a full deck. What is the chance that all three share a suit?

options.why: You named one suit and dealt with replacement.
You dealt with replacement, so each later card matched with chance $\tfrac14$.
You found the chance of three hearts, one named suit.

feedback.correct: The first card sets the suit, then $\tfrac{12}{51} \cdot \tfrac{11}{50}$.
feedback.generic: Let the first card choose the suit. Then the others must match it.

explain.text: The first card sets the suit; then $\tfrac{12}{51} \cdot \tfrac{11}{50} = \tfrac{22}{425}$. Counting hands: $4\binom{13}{3} = 1144$ of $\binom{52}{3} = 22100$ agree.

items.title: One reroll
items.question: You roll a fair die. You may roll once more, and then must keep the second face. Playing well, what is the expected face you keep?

options.why: You kept the better of two rolls. Once you reroll, you must keep the new face.
You ignored the reroll. That is the average of one roll.
You kept a 3 as well. A 3 is below the reroll's average of 3.5.

feedback.correct: Keep 4, 5 or 6; reroll the rest for an average of 3.5.
feedback.generic: Keep a face only if it beats the average of a fresh roll.

explain.text: Keep 4, 5 or 6, and reroll 1, 2 or 3 for 3.5 on average. So $\tfrac{4 + 5 + 6}{6} + \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac72 = \tfrac{17}{4}$. Trying every keep rule gives the same best.

items.title: Three days of the week
items.question: Three people are each born on a random day of the week. What is the chance that all three days differ?

options.why: You found the chance that two or more share a day.
You took off $\tfrac17$ for each of three pairs. The pairs overlap, so that is not exact.
You used only the third person's chance.

feedback.correct: $1 \cdot \tfrac67 \cdot \tfrac57$: each new person avoids the days taken.
feedback.generic: Seat the people one at a time. Each must avoid the days already used.

explain.text: The second avoids one day and the third avoids two: $\tfrac67 \cdot \tfrac57 = \tfrac{30}{49}$. Counting: $7 \cdot 6 \cdot 5 = 210$ of $7^3 = 343$ triples.

items.title: First six on the third
items.question: A fair die is rolled until the first six. What is the chance that the first six comes on the third roll?

options.why: You made every roll a six.
You used only the third roll. The first two must miss as well.
You found at least one six in three rolls.

feedback.correct: Two misses then a six: $(\tfrac56)^2 \cdot \tfrac16$.
feedback.generic: Write the rolls in order: what must the first two do?

explain.text: The first two rolls miss and the third hits: $\tfrac56 \cdot \tfrac56 \cdot \tfrac16 = \tfrac{25}{216}$. Listing 216 outcomes gives 25 of that shape.

items.title: Two quants of three
items.question: A desk of 5 traders and 4 quants picks a team of 3 at random. What is the chance of exactly 2 quants?

options.why: You picked with replacement, as if one person could be chosen twice.
You counted one order only, quant, quant, trader. There are 3 orders.
You found the chance of anything but exactly 2 quants.

feedback.correct: $\binom42 \binom51 = 30$ teams of $\binom93 = 84$.
feedback.generic: Count the teams that fit, then divide by all teams.

explain.text: Choose 2 of 4 quants and 1 of 5 traders: $6 \cdot 5 = 30$ of $\binom93 = 84$ teams, so $\tfrac{5}{14}$. Listing all 84 teams finds the same 30.

items.title: One of each colour
items.question: An urn holds 3 red and 2 blue balls. You draw 2 without replacement. What is the chance of one of each colour?

options.why: You counted one order only, red then blue.
You drew with replacement. The second draw has one ball fewer.
You found the chance of two of one colour.

feedback.correct: Red then blue or blue then red: $2 \cdot \tfrac35 \cdot \tfrac24$.
feedback.generic: Add the two orders, each without replacement.

explain.text: Red then blue is $\tfrac35 \cdot \tfrac24 = \tfrac{3}{10}$, and blue then red is the same. So the chance is $\tfrac35$. Counting: $\binom31\binom21 = 6$ of $\binom52 = 10$ pairs.

items.title: Flagged traders
items.question: 5% of traders have an edge. A screen flags 90% of those, and 10% of the rest. A trader is flagged. What is the chance they have an edge?

options.why: You gave the base rate and ignored the flag.
You gave the hit rate: the chance of a flag given an edge.
You divided the true flags by everyone, not by everyone flagged.

feedback.correct: Of 1,000 traders, 45 true flags and 95 false: $\tfrac{45}{140}$.
feedback.generic: Picture 1,000 traders. How many are flagged, and how many of those have an edge?

explain.text: In 1,000 traders, 50 have an edge and 45 are flagged; 950 do not and 95 are flagged. So $\tfrac{45}{140} = \tfrac{9}{28}$. Bayes' rule gives $\tfrac{0.045}{0.045 + 0.095}$, the same.

items.title: The larger face is 4
items.question: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the chance that the larger face is 4? (A double 4 counts.)

options.why: You treated the six values of the larger face as equally likely.
You found the chance that both are at most 4. Take away both at most 3.
You counted unordered pairs, so (1, 4) and (4, 1) became one.

feedback.correct: Both at most 4, less both at most 3: $\tfrac{16 - 9}{36}$.
feedback.generic: Find the chance that both are at most 4, then take away both at most 3.

explain.text: Both at most 4 has 16 pairs; both at most 3 has 9. So the larger is exactly 4 in 7 pairs: $\tfrac{7}{36}$. Listing the 36 pairs finds the same 7.

items.title: A 6, given 8
items.question: Two fair dice are rolled and the total is 8. What is the chance that at least one die shows 6?

options.why: You ignored the total. That is the chance of a 6 on any roll.
You listed unordered pairs as equally likely. Ordered pairs are.
You did not condition. That is the chance of the total and a 6 together.

feedback.correct: 2 of the 5 ordered pairs that make 8 show a 6.
feedback.generic: List the ordered pairs that make 8. Count those with a 6.

explain.text: The total 8 comes from (2, 6), (3, 5), (4, 4), (5, 3), (6, 2). Two of those 5 show a 6, so $\tfrac{2}{5}$.

items.title: First six wins
items.question: You and a friend take turns to roll a die, you first. The first to roll a six wins. What is your chance of winning?

options.why: You ignored going first. The first roller has the edge.
You counted only your first roll.
You found your friend's chance.

feedback.generic: Win now, or both miss and the game starts again.

explain.text: Let $p$ be your chance: $p = \tfrac16 + \tfrac{25}{36}p$, so $p = \tfrac{6}{11}$. The series $\tfrac16 \sum (\tfrac{25}{36})^k$ gives the same.

items.title: HH or TH
items.question: A fair coin is tossed until HH or TH appears. What is the chance that HH comes first?

options.why: You listed three cases as equally likely.
You treated the two patterns as equal. They are not: a T sets up TH.
You found the chance that TH comes first.

feedback.correct: HH wins only if the first two tosses are HH.
feedback.generic: What happens once the first T appears?

explain.text: Once a T appears, the next H completes TH before any HH. So HH wins only on HH at the start, with chance $\tfrac14$. An exact solve over the coin's states gives $\tfrac14$ too.

items.title: Rank three events
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: At least one six in 4 rolls of a die
At least one double six in 24 rolls of two dice
At least 6 heads in 10 tosses of a coin

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.518, 0.491, 0.377.
feedback.generic: Work out each chance roughly; a complement is often quickest.

explain.text: At least one six in 4 rolls of a die: 0.518. At least one double six in 24 rolls of two dice: 0.491. At least 6 heads in 10 tosses of a coin: 0.377.

items.title: Rank three events
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: Exactly 2 heads in 4 tosses of a coin
Two cards from a deck share a suit
A total of 7 on two dice

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.375, 0.235, 0.167.
feedback.generic: Turn each event into a fraction, then compare.

explain.text: Exactly 2 heads in 4 tosses of a coin: 0.375. Two cards from a deck share a suit: 0.235. A total of 7 on two dice: 0.167.

items.title: Rank three events
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: At least one six in 3 rolls of a die
A total of 6, 7 or 8 on two dice
Two cards from a deck differ in colour

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.510, 0.444, 0.421.
feedback.generic: Use complements for the at-least-one events, and do not add chances.

explain.text: Two cards from a deck differ in colour: 0.510. A total of 6, 7 or 8 on two dice: 0.444. At least one six in 3 rolls of a die: 0.421.

items.title: Rank three events
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.500, 0.312, 0.246.
feedback.generic: Count the ways for each, then divide by the outcomes.

explain.text: Exactly 1 head in 2 tosses: 0.500. Exactly 3 heads in 6 tosses: 0.312. Exactly 5 heads in 10 tosses: 0.246.

items.title: Rank three events
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: Two of 23 people share a birthday
Three dice all show different faces
At least one ace in 5 cards dealt from a deck

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.556, 0.507, 0.341.
feedback.generic: Estimate each with a complement: one minus the chance of none.

explain.text: Three dice all show different faces: 0.556. Two of 23 people share a birthday: 0.507. At least one ace in 5 cards dealt from a deck: 0.341.

items.title: Rank three events
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: At least one six in 6 rolls of a die
At least two sixes in 12 rolls of a die
At least three sixes in 18 rolls of a die

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.665, 0.619, 0.597.
feedback.generic: Do not assume the events tie because the expected counts match.

explain.text: At least one six in 6 rolls of a die: 0.665. At least two sixes in 12 rolls of a die: 0.619. At least three sixes in 18 rolls of a die: 0.597.

items.title: A square root
items.question: Choose the tightest interval that holds $\sqrt{300}$.

options.why: This holds the value, but 17 to 18 holds it too and is tighter. A wider interval scores less on the day.
This sits wholly below the value, 17.32.
This sits wholly above the value, 17.32.

feedback.correct: 17 to 18 holds the value, 17.32, and is the tightest that does.
feedback.generic: Bracket the value from both sides first, then pick the narrowest interval that holds it.

explain.text: $17^2 = 289$ and $18^2 = 324$, so $\sqrt{300}$ lies between 17 and 18. In fact $\sqrt{300} = 10\sqrt3 \approx 17.32$. The interval 15 to 20 holds it too, but it is wider, so it scores less on the day.

items.title: Compound growth
items.question: Choose the tightest interval that holds $1.05^{14}$.

options.why: This holds the value, but 1.9 to 2.0 holds it too and is tighter. A wider interval scores less on the day.
This sits wholly below the value, 1.98.
This sits wholly above the value, 1.98.

feedback.correct: 1.9 to 2.0 holds the value, 1.98, and is the tightest that does.
feedback.generic: Bracket the value from both sides first, then pick the narrowest interval that holds it.

explain.text: By the rule of 72, 5% a year doubles money in about 14.4 years. So 14 years gives just under 2; the exact value is 1.980. The interval 1.5 to 2.5 holds it too, but it is wider, so it scores less.

items.title: No six in twelve
items.question: A die is rolled 12 times. Choose the tightest interval that holds the chance of no six, $(\tfrac56)^{12}$.

options.why: This holds the value, but 0.10 to 0.12 holds it too and is tighter. A wider interval scores less on the day.
This sits wholly below the value, 0.1122.
This sits wholly above the value, 0.1122.

feedback.correct: 0.10 to 0.12 holds the value, 0.1122, and is the tightest that does.
feedback.generic: Bracket the value from both sides first, then pick the narrowest interval that holds it.

explain.text: $(\tfrac56)^6 \approx 0.335$, and squaring gives about 0.112. The exact value is 0.1122. The interval 0.05 to 0.25 holds it too, but it is wider, so it scores less.

items.title: Growth over 100 periods
items.question: £1 grows by 2% a period for 100 periods. Choose the tightest interval that holds its value in pounds, $1.02^{100}$.

options.why: This holds the value, but 7.0 to 7.5 holds it too and is tighter. A wider interval scores less on the day.
This sits wholly below the value, 7.245.
This sits wholly above the value, 7.245.

feedback.correct: 7.0 to 7.5 holds the value, 7.245, and is the tightest that does.
feedback.generic: Bracket the value from both sides first, then pick the narrowest interval that holds it.

explain.text: $\ln 1.02 \approx 0.0198$, so $1.02^{100} \approx e^{1.98} \approx 7.24$. Using $e^2 \approx 7.39$ alone lands in the same interval. The interval 5 to 10 holds it too, but it is wider, so it scores less.

parts.name: I used no calculator
parts.detail: Tick this only if you sat all three papers without one.
